summary: This experimental memo describes a simple means to associate arbitrary text strings with names, using the Domain Name System to store attributes that DNS does not otherwise define.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1464 proposes storing named text attributes in DNS TXT records. A program can look up an attribute by its name and receive its text value.

questions: how to extend dns with custom attributes
how to store attributes in dns
what is the dns txt attribute format
are dns attribute names case sensitive
subtitle: A proposal to store named text attributes in DNS TXT records.

tldr.problem: DNS normally stores information with predefined types, while applications may want to associate other text attributes with a name.
tldr.mechanism: The memo uses a DNS TXT record whose text contains an attribute name, an equals sign, and the attribute value.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1464 describes an experimental approach and says it requires no change to most existing DNS servers.

today: RFC 1464 is Experimental. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Using TXT Records for Attributes
sections.content: DNS is designed to store information with predefined types and structures, such as host addresses and mail exchanger names. RFC 1464 proposes using the existing TXT resource record to associate arbitrary ASCII text with attributes not defined as DNS record types. The memo says this approach requires no change to most existing DNS servers and does not replace the process for defining new resource records.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has standard record types for common information. This proposal uses TXT records to attach other named text values.

sections.title: Attribute Name and Value
sections.content: The TXT data uses the attribute name followed by an equals sign and its value. The first unquoted equals sign separates the name from the value; later characters belong to the value. Attribute names are case-insensitive. A backquote is used to quote an equals sign or backquote inside a name, and leading or trailing whitespace in names is ignored unless quoted.
sections.plainLanguage: The text has the form name=value. The first unquoted equals sign divides the attribute name from its value.

sections.title: Looking Up Attributes
sections.content: Attributes can be accessed through the standard resolver library, though the memo recommends a routine designed for this format. Such a routine could take an object name and attribute name, then return the value with quoting characters removed. The memo suggests that a registration process for well-known attribute names might help interoperability, but does not define one.
sections.plainLanguage: A program looks up a name and an attribute, then receives the stored value. This memo does not set a process for registering attribute names.
